summary: Describes HTCP, a protocol for discovering HTTP caches and cached data, managing sets of caches, and monitoring cache activity. It is one of several experimental proposals for this job.

plainLanguage.summary: Web caches keep copies of pages. This lets caches ask each other what they have, like neighbors lending books.

subtitle: A protocol for web caches to discover each other and share information about cached content.

tldr.problem: HTTP caches need to communicate with each other to discover what content each cache holds and to manage cache entries across a network of caches.
tldr.mechanism: HTCP defines a message-based protocol that allows caches to query each other for cached content, monitor cache changes, request deletions, and share metadata about objects.
tldr.outcome: This experimental protocol was one of several proposals for cache-to-cache communication, but did not become a standard. ICP (Internet Cache Protocol) and later approaches became more prevalent.

today: RFC 2756 is an Experimental protocol and has not been obsoleted or updated. HTCP remains a theoretical approach to cache communication, though it never achieved widespread deployment. Other mechanisms such as DNS-based service discovery and application-specific protocols became more common for cache coordination.

sections.title: What HTCP Does
sections.content:
RFC 2756 defines the Hyper Text Caching Protocol (HTCP), a protocol that allows HTTP caches (proxies) to communicate with each other. Unlike its predecessor ICP (Internet Cache Protocol), which could only examine URIs, HTCP includes full HTTP request and response headers in its queries. This allows caches to make more informed decisions about whether they actually hold a requested object, since the same URI might be cached in multiple forms depending on headers like Accept or Cookie.

HTCP enables cache discovery, content lookup, deletion requests, monitoring of cache activity, and sharing of hints about web objects such as alternative cache locations.
sections.plainLanguage: HTCP lets web caches talk to each other using full details about what they want, not just web addresses. This way a cache can ask 'do you have this page for a user with these preferences?' instead of just 'do you have this URL?'

sections.title: Messages and Protocol Structure
sections.content:
HTCP messages are sent over UDP (which must be supported) or optionally over TCP, using port 4827. Each message consists of a header, a data section, and an optional authentication section.

The header contains the total message length and version numbers (major and minor). The data section contains an operation code (OPCODE), a response code, a transaction ID, and operation-specific data. Optional authentication uses HMAC-MD5 with a timestamp and expiration time to prevent unauthorized cache manipulation.

All multi-byte values use network byte order, and messages should be treated with flexibility to handle network delays, reordering, or damage. Agents maintain configuration variables for maximum unacknowledged transactions and timeout intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: An HTCP message is like a letter: it says what action you want, includes a unique ID so you know which reply is for you, and can optionally be signed so only trusted caches can read it.

sections.title: Cache Operations
sections.content:
HTCP defines five main operations:

NOP (ping) tests basic connectivity. TST (test) queries whether a cache holds a specific object using full request headers; the response includes the object's headers if present. MON (monitor) subscribes to a stream of notifications about a cache's local activity such as adds, refreshes, replacements, or deletions. SET pushes information about an object to a cache, allowing caches to share updated headers or hints about other cache locations. CLR (clear) tells a cache to delete a specific object or all objects with a given URI.

Each operation has its own set of response codes. For example, TST responds with 0 (entity is in cache) or 1 (entity is not in cache).
sections.plainLanguage: TST is 'do you have this?', MON is 'tell me when things change', SET is 'here's something useful to know', and CLR is 'delete this'.

sections.title: Cache-Specific Headers
sections.content:
Beyond standard HTTP headers, HTCP introduces cache-specific headers that caches can use to share additional information about cached objects:

Cache-Vary overrides the object's Vary header with a learned set of headers that affect cacheability. Cache-Location lists other caches that hold copies, useful for discovery. Cache-Policy carries caching rules beyond what HTTP headers express, such as no-cache, no-share, or no-cache-cookie. Cache-Flags marks incomplete responses. Cache-Expiry overrides the object's expiration time. Cache-MD5 supplies a computed checksum. Cache-to-Origin reports measured round-trip time, sample count, and hop count to an origin server.
sections.plainLanguage: These extra headers let caches tell each other 'this object changes based on cookies', 'I also have it at server X', or 'this took 50ms to fetch'.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content: Without the optional AUTH element, HTCP traffic is vulnerable. Any third party can query a cache to discover what it holds, and can send SET or CLR messages to modify or delete cached content. The optional authentication mechanism uses a shared secret and HMAC-MD5 to cryptographically sign messages with timestamps and expiration windows. Shared secrets should be cryptographically generated and at least a few hundred octets long to resist attack. When authentication is enabled, both the request and response validate that the sender is authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: Without signing, anyone on your network can pretend to be a trusted cache and tell yours to delete things. Signing makes caches prove they know a shared secret.
